Persona Conversation Simulator · guide

Big Five personality traits and conflict: who clashes, and why

Most arguments between colleagues, housemates or a buyer and a seller are not about personality. But personality shapes how a disagreement goes: who speaks first, who gives way, who holds a line, and when it boils over. This page sets out the rules the simulator uses to turn the five broad traits into those tendencies. The rules are written out so you can check them and disagree with them.

The five traits, in conversation

TraitHighLow
OpennessReframes the problem, pushes new optionsWants proof it has worked before
ConscientiousnessWants a plan, dates and ownersImprovises, moves on before details settle
ExtraversionSpeaks first and most, thinks aloudSpeaks later and less, better in writing
AgreeablenessSeeks common ground, concedes to keep the peaceBlunt, sceptical, holds a hard line
NeuroticismFeels pressure quickly, can escalateCalm, hard to provoke

From traits to a conflict style

The Thomas-Kilmann model sorts conflict behaviour on two axes: how hard you push for your own outcome (assertiveness), and how much you try to meet the other person's needs (cooperativeness). That gives five styles: competing, collaborating, compromising, accommodating and avoiding. The simulator approximates the two axes from the Big Five:

  • Assertiveness = 0.6 × extraversion + 0.4 × (100 − agreeableness)
  • Cooperativeness = 0.75 × agreeableness + 0.25 × openness

Both near the middle reads as compromising. Otherwise the quadrant picks the style. This is a heuristic mapping written for the tool, not a validated psychometric conversion.

Which trait gaps cause friction

  • Two low-agreeableness people. Two hard lines and little giving way. This is the strongest friction signal the tool uses.
  • Two high-neuroticism people. Small disagreements escalate quickly. A calm partner (low neuroticism) steadies an anxious one instead.
  • A wide agreeableness gap. The softer person may concede more than they meant to.
  • A wide conscientiousness gap. A planner and an improviser argue about pace and detail more than about the goal.
  • A wide extraversion gap. Rarely open conflict, but the quieter person's view surfaces late or not at all. Ask them directly.
  • Shared high openness or conscientiousness counts as rapport: good at finding a third option, or at leaving with owners and dates.

Research on bargaining points the same way for agreeableness and extraversion. In a straight haggle over one number, both traits have been found to be liabilities rather than strengths (Barry and Friedman, 1998, on distributive negotiation). The simulator's concession sizes follow that direction. Its exact weights are hand-set, not fitted to any study.

Worked example: same two people, roles swapped

Two invented characters. Rosa Juniper scores O70 C80 E75 A20 N30. Linus Oakhaven scores O40 C30 E20 A80 N70. The tool rates the pair high friction:

  • Rosa is far blunter than Linus; Linus may concede more than they meant to.
  • Rosa will take most of the airtime; Linus's view may surface late or not at all.
  • Rosa wants a plan and dates; Linus wants to keep it loose. Pace and detail are the likely sore point.
  • Rosa's calm can steady Linus when things get tense.

Run the salary negotiation 500 times with seed guide, then swap who is the candidate:

CandidateHiring managerDeal reachedMedian salary when they agree
RosaLinus57%$118,000
LinusRosa53%$102,000

With the same two people and the same budgets, the median deal moves by $16,000 depending on which side the blunt, assertive character sits. In both directions the deal lands near the edge of Linus's range. That is the rehearsal point. If you concede easily, decide your limit before the conversation, and say less after you have made your offer.

Build your own cast and run it

Which Big Five traits matter most in a conflict?

Agreeableness and neuroticism do the most work. Agreeableness sets how readily someone gives way, and neuroticism sets how quickly pressure turns into escalation. Extraversion decides who holds the floor, and conscientiousness and openness show up as arguments about pace, detail and new ideas.

Which personality pairs clash the most?

Two low-agreeableness people (two hard lines), two high-neuroticism people (fast escalation), and pairs with a wide conscientiousness gap (a planner and an improviser arguing about pace and detail). A wide extraversion gap rarely causes open conflict, but the quieter person's view tends to surface late or not at all.

What this is not

Trait scores describe broad tendencies across many people. They do not tell you what one person will do on a given day, and nothing here is a way to assess a real person. The simulator builds invented characters only and refuses profile links, handles and contact details.

No warranty. This guide and the simulator are provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. They are not psychological, medical, HR, legal or career advice, and not a personality assessment of anyone. PERSONA CONVERSATION SIMULATOR · FICTIONAL CHARACTERS · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Simulate conversations between fictional personalities

Invent a cast of two to six characters, give each a Big Five personality (or describe them in a sentence), and see their conflict style, who will clash and why. Then play out a salary negotiation, a team meeting or a housemates' argument between them, once to read the transcript or hundreds of times to see how often each outcome happens.

Fictional characters only. This is not a way to profile or clone a real person: it takes no profile links, handles or contact details, and the names it generates are invented. Use it to rehearse a hard conversation, think about team dynamics, or write characters. Everything runs in this browser and nothing is uploaded.

1. Your cast

2. How they are likely to get on

3. Run a scenario

Optional: write the lines in each character's voice with your own AI key

The rules decide who speaks, what they do and every number. This pass only rewrites the wording of each line, and any rewrite that drops or changes a number is thrown away. It sends the character cards and the transcript straight from this browser to the provider you pick. Your key stays in this browser and is never sent to us. A model on your own computer (Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp) needs no key.

Pick a scenario and press play.

Transcript

Across many runs

What you use today, and what this does differently

Personality tests describe one person and stop there. Chatbot role-play gives you a fluent conversation, but a different one every time and with no way to see why a character gave way. This tool keeps the rules in the open: trait scores set the odds of each move, the same seed replays the same conversation, and running a cast hundreds of times shows how often a deal closes or a meeting falls apart. It is a way to think about how people tend to differ, not a substitute for talking to the real ones.

Run it from the command line

Zero dependencies, Node 18+. A cast file is a JSON list of invented characters: [{"name": "Ava Juniper", "role": "founder", "description": "blunt, organised, calm"}].

node cli.mjs --list
node cli.mjs --scenario salary --seed 7 --runs 500
node cli.mjs --scenario team-deadline --cast cast.json --format json

Questions people actually ask

Can I simulate a conversation between different personality types?

Yes. Give two to six invented characters Big Five scores (or describe them in a sentence), pick a scenario such as a salary negotiation or a team meeting, and the simulator plays it out turn by turn. Run it hundreds of times to see how often each outcome happens with that cast.

Can I make a digital clone of a real person from their social media?

No. This tool only builds invented characters. Profiling a real person from scraped profiles without their consent raises privacy, legal and platform-terms problems, and a confident personality read of someone who never took a test is not accurate anyway. The tool refuses profile links, handles and contact details.

How does the simulator decide what each character says?

With fixed rules you can read in sim.mjs. Each turn it picks who speaks, weighted towards extraversion and whoever was just asked, and what they do: propose, object, concede, ask, hold firm or walk away, with odds set by their trait scores and how tense the conversation is. The same seed and cast always give the same transcript.

Does it predict how real people would behave?

No. The weights are hand-set to follow broad tendencies, such as agreeable people conceding more and anxious people escalating under pressure. They are not fitted to data. Use it to rehearse and to think about a group's dynamics, not to forecast what a particular person will do.

Do I need an AI key?

No. The simulator runs entirely on rules in your browser. An optional pass on your own Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini or local model rewrites each line in the character's voice, but it cannot change who speaks, what they do or any number.

Longer version: Big Five personality traits and conflict: who clashes, and why.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is a rules-based simulation of invented characters, not psychological, medical, HR, legal or career advice, and not a personality assessment of anyone. It does not predict what any real person will do. You are responsible for how you use its output. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Download your cast if you want to keep it, or get sim.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. Your characters are never uploaded unless you turn on the optional AI pass with your own key; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors, and without that pass the page makes no network calls. Anonymous feature events (sim_run, many_run, character_added, export_used) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.
